claims.text: Handir's father, Haldir, joined the Union of Maedhros, and led many Men of Brethil to the Battle of Unnumbered Tears. As the battle turned against Eldar and the Edain, Haldir was slain in the rearguard of Fingon, along with most of the Men of Brethil. Those that survived still had to find their way back through the evil road of Taur-nu-Fuin, and in the end only three Men who had accompanied Haldir returned, healed of their wounds and brought back by Mablung.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Fifth Battle: Nirnaeth Arnoediad"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Departure of Túrin"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part Three. The Wanderings of Húrin and Other Writings not forming part of the Quenta Silmarillion: I. The Wanderings of Húrin"

claims.text: It is not said if Handir was among those who joined the battle, but with the death of his father, he became the leader of the Haladin. News of his father's death also caused his mother, Glóredhel, to fall into grief and die.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Departure of Túrin"

claims.text: Around a large group of Orcs crossed the Brithiach. Though Handir resisted them with all the force he could muster, they continued and passed south over the Crossings of Teiglin in search of plunder.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "Túrin among the Outlaws"

claims.text: Starting in the Elves of Nargothrond, under the leadership of Túrin, went openly to battle and drove the Orcs out of West Beleriand; in doing so however they revealed themselves to the wrath of Morgoth. In the spring of , the Orcs invaded the lands of Handir in order to secure the Crossings of Teiglin in preparation for an assault against Nargothrond. Handir gave them battle, but he was slain and his folk driven back into the woods. The Orcs did not pursue them, and continued to muster their strength until their assault against Nargothrond that autumn.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §272; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §295; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Fall of Nargothrond"

claims.text: With the death of Handir, his son Brandir became the next chieftain.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §291

claims.text: In Turambar and the Foalókë, Bethos was a stout man and the chief of the wood-rangers with whom Túrin dwelt. As a youth, he had fought in, and escaped from, the Battle of Unnumbered Tears. His wife, "as the tale telleth", was a fair Noldo-maiden and they had many fair sons and daughters save their eldest, Tamar Lamefoot.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "II. Turambar and the Foalókë"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > The Book of Lost Tales

claims.text: When Túrin brought a rescued Níniel back to their settlement, she dwelt in the house of Bethos. Bethos himself was slain not long after in an foray as, despite his years, he still rode abroad. Túrin was then chosen as the new chief of the wood-rangers, rather than Tamar.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "II. Turambar and the Foalókë"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > The Book of Lost Tales

claims.text: In Christopher Tolkien's commentary, he noted the extraordinary statement that Bethos had a Elven wife, and that it contradicted the statement elsewhere that Eärendel alone was a child of both races. Christopher also notes the discrepancy of Bethos being "but a boy" at the Battle of Unnumbered Tears, and considered old ("despite his years") at the time of his death.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "II. Turambar and the Foalókë": "Notes and Commentary"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > The Book of Lost Tales

claims.text: In The Quenta, Handir became the father of Brandir. Handir was the son of Haleth, who in turn was the son of Hador.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Shaping of Middle-earth, "III. The Quenta: Commentary on the Quenta, [Section] 13"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > The Shaping of Middle-earth

claims.text: In The Earliest Annals of Beleriand, Handir became the son of Hundor, son of Haleth. Between the years 190-195, Handir allied his people with the Gnomes of Nargothrond who, led by Túrin, drove the Orcs from West Beleriand. He was slain when Glómund and a host of Orcs defeated the forces of Nargothrond.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Shaping of Middle-earth, "VII. The Earliest Annals of Beleriand: [The first version of The Earliest Annals of Beleriand (Text AB I)]"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > The Shaping of Middle-earth

claims.text: In a struck-out passage, it was Handir who accompanied Húrin when, by the fate or will of Ulmo, they found the hidden entrance to Gondolin. They were welcomed by Turgon and eventually released after swearing oaths of secrecy of the location of the city.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §§149–50
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > The War of the Jewels
